notes:
Continuity

  • $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)$.
  • Sum, difference, product, quotient (denominator $\ne0$) and composition of continuous functions are continuous.
  • Polynomial, $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $e^x$ are continuous everywhere; $\tan x$ is discontinuous where $\cos x=0$; $|x|$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at $0$.

Differentiability

  • $f$ is differentiable at $a$ if $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ exists (left derivative = right derivative).
  • Differentiability $\Rightarrow$ continuity, but not conversely (e.g. $|x|$ at $0$).

Differentiation rules

FunctionDerivative
$x^n$$nx^{n-1}$
$\sin x,\ \cos x$$\cos x,\ -\sin x$
$\tan x$$\sec^2x$
$e^x,\ a^x$$e^x,\ a^x\ln a$
$\ln x$$1/x$
$\sin^{-1}x$$1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$
$\tan^{-1}x$$1/(1+x^2)$
  • Product rule: $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$. Quotient rule: $\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$.
  • Chain rule: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy}{dt}\cdot\dfrac{dt}{dx}$.
  • Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides w.r.t. $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$ (use chain rule for $y$ terms).
  • Logarithmic differentiation: for $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$, take $\ln$ both sides then differentiate: $\dfrac{y'}{y}=g'(x)\ln f(x)+g(x)\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
  • Parametric: if $x=f(t),\,y=g(t)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$.

Higher order derivatives & key theorems

  • $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is the derivative of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ w.r.t. $x$.
  • Rolle's theorem: if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $f(a)=f(b)$, then $\exists\,c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$.
  • Mean Value Theorem: under the same continuity/differentiability conditions, $\exists\,c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 3-4 questions from this chapter — checking continuity/differentiability at a point, standard derivative rules (chain, product, implicit, parametric, logarithmic), and occasionally Rolle's/MVT value of $c$. Master differentiating $\sin^{-1},\cos^{-1},\tan^{-1}$ composite forms — they appear often.

questions.explanation: $|x|$ has left derivative $-1$ and right derivative $+1$ at $0$, unequal so not differentiable; but $\lim_{x\to0}|x|=0=f(0)$, so it is continuous.
questions.trick: $|x|$ is always continuous but never differentiable at the corner point.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\begin{cases}kx+1,&x\le5\\3x-5,&x>5\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=5$, then $k$ equals
questions.explanation: Need $5k+1=3(5)-5=10\Rightarrow5k=9\Rightarrow k=9/5$.
questions.trick: Equate the left piece and right piece at the join point, then solve.

questions.explanation: By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)=\cos(x^2)\cdot2x$.
questions.trick: Chain rule: derivative of the outer function times derivative of the inner.

questions.explanation: Take $\ln$: $\ln y=x\ln x$. Differentiate: $y'/y=\ln x+1$, so $y'=x^x(\ln x+1)$.
questions.trick: Variable base AND exponent $\Rightarrow$ take $\ln$ first (logarithmic differentiation).

questions.explanation: $dx/dt=2at$, $dy/dt=2a$. $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2a}{2at}=\dfrac{1}{t}$.
questions.trick: Parametric: divide $dy/dt$ by $dx/dt$.

questions.q: If $x^2+y^2=25$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $(3,4)$ is
questions.explanation: Differentiating implicitly: $2x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-x/y=-3/4$.
questions.trick: Implicit differentiation on a circle gives $dy/dx=-x/y$.

questions.explanation: Standard derivative formula: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x=\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$.
questions.trick: Memorize: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$.

questions.q: For Rolle's theorem to be applicable to $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$ on $[1,3]$, the value of $c$ is
questions.explanation: $f(1)=0=f(3)$, so Rolle's applies. $f'(x)=2x-4=0\Rightarrow x=2\in(1,3)$.
questions.trick: Rolle's: after checking $f(a)=f(b)$, just solve $f'(x)=0$ inside $(a,b)$.

questions.q: By the Mean Value Theorem, for $f(x)=x^2$ on $[1,4]$, the value of $c$ is
questions.trick: MVT: set $f'(c)$ equal to the average slope $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, solve.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log(\sin x)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\cot x$.
questions.trick: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log(\sin x)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\cot x$.
Differentiate twice; each chain-rule step brings down another factor of $2$.

questions.explanation: The function is undefined (denominator zero) at $x=2$, so it is discontinuous there; it is continuous everywhere else in its domain.
questions.trick: A rational function is discontinuous exactly where its denominator vanishes.

questions.explanation: For $|x|\le1$, $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)=2\tan^{-1}x$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}$.
questions.trick: Spot the disguised double-angle: $\sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)=2\tan^{-1}x$ for $|x|\le1$.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3u^2\cdot3=9u^2$. At $x=1$, $u=2$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=9\times4=36$.
questions.trick: Chain rule $dy/dx=dy/du\cdot du/dx$, then substitute the $x$-value last.

questions.q: The derivative of $\log_{10}x$ with respect to $x$ is
questions.explanation: $\log_{10}x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln10}$, so its derivative is $\dfrac{1}{x\ln10}$.
questions.trick: Convert $\log_a x$ to $\ln x/\ln a$ before differentiating.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sin x}{x},&x\ne0\\k,&x=0\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $k$ equals
questions.explanation: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x}=1$, so $k$ must equal $1$ for continuity.
questions.trick: Standard limit $\sin x/x\to1$ as $x\to0$ fixes $k$ for continuity.

questions.explanation: $y=(\sin x)^{1/2}$; by chain rule $y'=\dfrac12(\sin x)^{-1/2}\cos x=\dfrac{\cos x}{2\sqrt{\sin x}}$.
questions.trick: Write as $(\sin x)^{1/2}$ and apply the chain rule with the power rule.

questions.explanation: For $x\ge0$, $f(x)=x^2$; for $x<0$, $f(x)=-x^2$. Both left and right derivatives at $0$ equal $0$, so $f$ is differentiable there with $f'(0)=0$.
questions.trick: Split into cases ($x\ge0$, $x<0$) and check that left/right derivatives match.

questions.q: The number of points at which $f(x)=[x]$ (greatest integer function) is discontinuous in $(0,4)$ is
questions.explanation: $[x]$ jumps at every integer; within the open interval $(0,4)$ the integers are $1,2,3$, giving 3 points of discontinuity.
questions.trick: The greatest integer function jumps at every integer inside the interval.

questions.explanation: Putting $x=\cos\theta$, $2x^2-1=\cos2\theta$, so $y=2\theta=2\cos^{-1}x$. Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
questions.trick: Spot the disguised double-angle: $\cos^{-1}(2x^2-1)=2\cos^{-1}x$ for $0<x<1$.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\begin{cases}3x-2,&x<2\\2k,&x=2\\x+2,&x>2\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=2$, then $k$ equals
questions.explanation: Left limit $=3(2)-2=4$, right limit $=2+2=4$. For continuity, $f(2)=2k$ must equal this common limit: $2k=4\Rightarrow k=2$.
questions.trick: Match left limit $=$ right limit $=f(a)$, then solve for the unknown.

questions.explanation: Since $\left|x^2\sin\frac1x\right|\le x^2\to0$ as $x\to0$, $f$ is continuous at $0$. Also $f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h^2\sin(1/h)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}h\sin(1/h)=0$ exists, so $f$ is differentiable at $0$ too.
questions.trick: Squeeze theorem: bounded $\times\,x^2\to0$ gives both continuity and differentiability at $0$.

questions.explanation: By the product rule: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\cos x+e^x(-\sin x)=e^x(\cos x-\sin x)$.
questions.trick: Product rule: $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}=\dfrac{\frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}+x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$.
questions.trick: This is essentially $\sinh^{-1}x$ — its derivative simplifies to $1/\sqrt{x^2+1}$.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta$, $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=a\cos\theta$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta$.
questions.trick: Parametric circle: $dy/dx=-\cot\theta$, the ratio of the $\theta$-derivatives.

questions.q: If $y^x=x^y$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at a general point is given by which method?
options: Logarithmic differentiation (taking log on both sides)
questions.explanation: When the variable appears in both the base and exponent (as in $y^x=x^y$), taking logarithms first (logarithmic differentiation) makes the differentiation tractable.
questions.trick: Variable exponents on both sides $\Rightarrow$ logarithmic differentiation.

questions.explanation: Since $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (a constant) for all $x\in[-1,1]$, its derivative is $0$.
questions.trick: Constant function ($\pi/2$) has derivative $0$ — no computation needed.

options: discontinuous at $x=1$ since left limit does not equal right limit
discontinuous at $x=1$ since left and right limits differ from $f(1)$
questions.explanation: Left limit $=1$, right limit $=2(1)+1=3$; since these two limits are unequal, $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ (regardless of $f(1)=5$).
questions.trick: Left limit $\ne$ right limit alone is enough to prove discontinuity.

options: continuous everywhere but not differentiable at $x=3$
questions.explanation: $|x-3|$ is continuous everywhere (no jumps), but it has a sharp corner at $x=3$ where the left derivative ($-1$) and right derivative ($1$) differ, so it is not differentiable there.
questions.trick: $|x-a|$ is always continuous but has a non-differentiable corner at $x=a$.

questions.explanation: Using the substitution $x=\tan\phi$, $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$, so $y=2\tan^{-1}x$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}$.
questions.trick: Spot the disguised double-angle: $\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)=2\tan^{-1}x$ for $|x|<1$.

questions.explanation: Differentiating implicitly: $2+3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos y\dfrac{dy}{dx}\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx}(\cos y-3)=2\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{\cos y-3}=\dfrac{-2}{3-\cos y}$.
questions.trick: Differentiate both sides w.r.t. $x$, then collect all $dy/dx$ terms on one side.

questions.q: If $y=(\sin x)^{\cos x}$, then which technique is essential to differentiate $y$?
questions.explanation: Since the base and exponent both involve $x$ (a variable raised to a variable power), taking logarithm first (logarithmic differentiation) is the standard technique.
questions.trick: Variable base AND variable exponent $\Rightarrow$ logarithmic differentiation is essential.

questions.q: If $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $f(a)=f(b)$, this is the hypothesis of
questions.explanation: These are exactly the conditions of Rolle's Theorem, which concludes that some $c\in(a,b)$ has $f'(c)=0$.
questions.trick: $f(a)=f(b)$ plus continuity/differentiability is exactly Rolle's setup.

questions.explanation: By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\log x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{1}{x\log x}$.
questions.trick: Chain rule twice: outer log, then inner log, multiply the two factors.

questions.explanation: For $y=a^x$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=a^x\ln a$; here $a=3$, giving $3^x\ln3$.
questions.trick: $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x=a^x\ln a$ — don't forget the $\ln a$ factor.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ for $x\ne2$ and $f(2)=k$, and $f$ is continuous at $x=2$, then $k$ equals
questions.explanation: $\lim_{x\to2}\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}=\lim_{x\to2}(x+2)=4$, so for continuity $k=4$.
questions.trick: Factor and cancel to find the removable-discontinuity limit value.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every differentiable function is continuous. Reason (R): Every continuous function is differentiable.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Differentiability always implies continuity, so A is true. But the converse is false (e.g. $|x|$ is continuous but not differentiable at $0$), so R is false.
questions.trick: Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous is TRUE; the converse is FALSE (e.g. $|x|$).

questions.explanation: By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos(\log x)\cdot\dfrac1x=\dfrac{\cos(\log x)}{x}$.
questions.trick: Chain rule: $\cos(\log x)$ times the derivative of $\log x$ (which is $1/x$).
Differentiate twice, then just substitute the given $x$ value.

questions.q: For $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2},&x\ne0\\k,&x=0\end{cases}$ to be continuous at $x=0$, $k$ equals
questions.explanation: $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2=\dfrac12$, so $k=\dfrac12$.
questions.trick: Use $1-\cos x=2\sin^2(x/2)$ to reduce to the standard limit $\sin\theta/\theta\to1$.

questions.q: The function $f(x)=|\cos x|$ is continuous everywhere but fails to be differentiable at
questions.explanation: $\cos x=0$ at $x=\pi/2$, where $\cos x$ changes sign, giving $|\cos x|$ a sharp corner there; left and right derivatives are $\mp\sin x=\mp1$, unequal. At $x=0,\pi,2\pi$, $\cos x=\pm1$ and $|\cos x|$ is smooth.
questions.trick: $|\cos x|$ has corners exactly where $\cos x=0$.

questions.q: The derivative of $\sin x$ with respect to $\log x$ is
questions.explanation: Let $u=\log x$. Then $\dfrac{d(\sin x)}{du}=\dfrac{d(\sin x)/dx}{du/dx}=\dfrac{\cos x}{1/x}=x\cos x$.
questions.trick: Derivative of $f$ w.r.t. $g$ equals $f'(x)/g'(x)$.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=-3a\cos^2\theta\sin\theta$, $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=3a\sin^2\theta\cos\theta$. Dividing gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=-\tan\theta$.
questions.trick: Astroid-type parametric curve: $dy/dx=-\tan\theta$.

questions.q: A function $f$ satisfies $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ for all $x,y$, with $f(0)\ne0$. If $f(3)=2$ and $f'(0)=4$, then $f'(3)$ equals
questions.explanation: Differentiating $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ with respect to $y$ and setting $y=0$ gives $f'(x)=f(x)f'(0)$. So $f'(3)=f(3)\cdot f'(0)=2\times4=8$.
questions.trick: For $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$, always $f'(x)=f(x)f'(0)$.

questions.q: Rolle's theorem is NOT applicable to $f(x)=|x|$ on $[-2,2]$, even though $f(-2)=f(2)=2$, because
questions.explanation: $|x|$ is continuous on $[-2,2]$ and $f(-2)=f(2)$, but it has a corner at $x=0$, an interior point, so $f$ fails to be differentiable on $(-2,2)$ — this violates Rolle's hypothesis.
questions.trick: A corner point inside $(a,b)$ blocks Rolle's theorem even if endpoints match.

questions.q: The function $f(x)=\cot x$ is discontinuous at every point of the set
questions.explanation: $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$ is undefined wherever $\sin x=0$, i.e. at $x=n\pi$, $n\in\mathbb Z$.
questions.trick: $\cot x$ blows up where $\sin x=0$ — integer multiples of $\pi$.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, then the composite function $f(f(x))$ is discontinuous at
questions.explanation: $f(f(x))=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{x-1}-1}=\dfrac{x-1}{2-x}$. This fails at $x=1$ (where $f(x)$ itself is undefined) and at $x=2$ (where the simplified denominator vanishes).
questions.trick: For $f(f(x))$, check both the original singularity and the new one after simplifying.

questions.explanation: $y'=3\cos x-4\sin x$. Then $y^2+y'^2=(3\sin x+4\cos x)^2+(3\cos x-4\sin x)^2=9+16=25$, since the cross terms cancel and $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
questions.trick: For $y=a\sin x+b\cos x$, $y^2+y'^2=a^2+b^2$, a constant.

questions.explanation: Take $\ln$: $\ln y=x\ln(\sin x)$. Differentiating, $y'/y=\ln(\sin x)+x\cdot\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\ln(\sin x)+x\cot x$, so $y'=(\sin x)^x[\ln(\sin x)+x\cot x]$.
questions.trick: Variable base and exponent: take log first, then use the product rule.

questions.explanation: At $x=0$: $e^y=e\Rightarrow y=1$. Differentiating implicitly: $e^yy'+y+xy'=0\Rightarrow y'(e^y+x)=-y$. At $x=0,y=1$: $y'\cdot e=-1\Rightarrow y'=-1/e$.
questions.trick: Find the point first (here $y=1$ when $x=0$), then differentiate implicitly.

questions.explanation: For $|x|\le1/2$, $\sin^{-1}(3x-4x^3)=3\sin^{-1}x$ (triple-angle identity), so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
questions.trick: Spot the disguised triple-angle: $\sin^{-1}(3x-4x^3)=3\sin^{-1}x$ for $|x|\le\tfrac12$.

questions.explanation: $f(1^-)=1=f(1^+)$, so $f$ is continuous. Left derivative $2x\to2$ and right derivative $2\to2$ agree, so $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$ with $f'(1)=2$.
questions.trick: Check that left and right derivatives are numerically equal, not just continuity.

questions.q: For $f(x)=\ln x$ on $[1,e]$, the value of $c$ guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem is
questions.explanation: $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(e)-f(1)}{e-1}=\dfrac{1-0}{e-1}=\dfrac{1}{e-1}$. Since $f'(x)=1/x$, $1/c=1/(e-1)\Rightarrow c=e-1$.
questions.trick: MVT slope for $\ln x$ over $[1,e]$ is $1/(e-1)$; solve $f'(c)=$ that.

questions.q: The derivative of $e^x$ with respect to $x^2$ is
questions.explanation: Let $u=x^2$. Then $\dfrac{d(e^x)}{du}=\dfrac{d(e^x)/dx}{du/dx}=\dfrac{e^x}{2x}$.
questions.trick: Derivative of $f$ w.r.t. $g$: divide $f'(x)$ by $g'(x)$.

questions.q: If $x^2+y^2=1$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at the point $(0,1)$ equals
questions.explanation: Differentiating: $2x+2yy'=0\Rightarrow y'=-x/y$. At $(0,1)$, $y'=0$. Differentiating again, $y''=-\dfrac{y-xy'}{y^2}$; at $(0,1)$, $y''=-\dfrac{1-0}{1}=-1$.
questions.trick: Differentiate implicitly twice; substitute the point only at the end.

questions.explanation: By the product rule, $y'=e^{x^2}\cdot2x\ln x+e^{x^2}\cdot\dfrac1x$. At $x=1$, $\ln1=0$, so $y'=e^1(0+1)=e$.
questions.trick: At $x=1$, $\ln x=0$ kills the first term — only $1/x$ survives.
Differentiate twice, substitute last — watch the constant $-4$.

questions.explanation: Standard derivative formula: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, opposite in sign to $\sin^{-1}x$'s derivative.
questions.trick: $\sin^{-1}x$ and $\cos^{-1}x$ have equal-magnitude, opposite-sign derivatives.
Differentiate term by term — only the linear term 'x' survives at $x=0$.

questions.q: If $f(x)$ is an even function (i.e. $f(-x)=f(x)$) and is differentiable, then $f'(x)$ is
options: neither even nor odd in general
questions.explanation: Differentiating $f(-x)=f(x)$ using the chain rule gives $-f'(-x)=f'(x)$, i.e. $f'(-x)=-f'(x)$ — the definition of an odd function.
questions.trick: Differentiate the even-function identity $f(-x)=f(x)$ to see the sign flip.
